venues.d: A time-capsule of the British Raj on the hill where Darjeeling began — coal fires, hot-water bottles, afternoon tea and the oldest heritage hotel in the Himalayas.
A hilltop heritage resort in the former summer palace of the Raja of Nazargunj — colonial fireplaces and carved wood, gardens, and a spa, opposite the Governor's House.

venues.n: Taj Chia Kutir Resort & Spa, Darjeeling
venues.d: Taj's tea-country resort inside the historic Makaibari estate — bamboo, timber and stone in the mist, with a spa, indoor pool and guided estate walks.
A 19th-century manor house turned five-star heritage hotel — Burma-teak floors, crackling fireplaces and a grand piano, once an Oberoi-family home.
A colonial-era boutique hideaway on a Kurseong ridge — a British magistrate's old house restored, with unobstructed Kanchenjunga views and an Anglo-Indian tea kitchen.
The finest meals in the hills are served at Glenburn — butler-hosted, produce from the estate, laid out on the verandah with Kanchenjunga in view.
A candle-lit heritage dining room with a grand piano — considered Anglo-Indian and regional cooking under oak panelling and old etchings.
The great colonial afternoon tea of the Himalayas — cucumber sandwiches, scones and Darjeeling tea by the fire, in the oldest heritage hotel in the hills.
Darjeeling's grand old café-bakery since the 1880s — a first-floor restaurant, a famous ground-floor bakery, and Kanchenjunga through the windows.
The 1911 rooftop breakfast institution — sausages, ham and eggs above the Mall, Kanchenjunga on the skyline, immortalised in Satyajit Ray's films.
The town's most-loved Tibetan kitchen — steaming momos and thukpa in a tiny, family-run room where you may have to wait for a seat.

venues.a: Dr Zakir Hussain Road, Darjeeling town
venues.d: A tiny café with a cult following — proper coffee, big breakfasts, and honest thukpa and momos, run by a local family.

Before dawn you climb to 2,590 m and wait in the cold dark until the first light strikes Kanchenjunga's summit and it turns rose, then gold, over the sleeping range; on the clearest mornings Everest itself is a faint tooth on the far horizon. A private car and a flask of first-flush tea turn the pre-4am pilgrimage into something you will still talk about years later.

venues.n: Darjeeling Himalayan Railway Toy Train Joy Ride
venues.d: The little blue steam engine of 1881 pulls you up through the town's rooftops, around the spiralling Batasia Loop and up to Ghum, India's highest station, at a walking pace that lets you lean out and be handed marigolds. It is pure Raj-era romance, and a joy that spans generations from a five-year-old to a grandfather who rode it as a boy.

The toy train coils through a full circle here around a landscaped garden while Kanchenjunga fills the sky behind the Gorkha soldiers' memorial. The train pauses ten minutes so you can walk the flower beds and take in the panorama; it is the single most photographed spot on the line.

At 2,258 m this is the highest railway station in India, its little first-floor museum lined with the brass fittings, old photographs and a vintage engine that tell the story of how the line was built. A short, atmospheric stop that gives the toy train its historical weight.

Founded in 1850, the oldest Tibetan monastery of the region shelters a serene fifteen-foot Maitreya Buddha in gold and vermilion, butter lamps glowing against ancient manuscripts. Quiet, incense-scented and deeply atmospheric, it rewards an unhurried private visit away from the town crowds.

Darjeeling's second-oldest garden, planted in 1854 on slopes just below the town, where you walk between the bushes with the pluckers and then sit for a proper tasting of the estate's organic first and second flush. It is the most accessible way to understand why Darjeeling tea is spoken of like a fine wine.

India's largest high-altitude zoo runs the country's flagship breeding programmes for the red panda and the snow leopard, and here you can actually watch a red panda curled in a fir tree at eye level. A genuine conservation landmark that captivates children and grandparents alike.

Founded after Tenzing Norgay's 1953 Everest summit and long led by him, the institute's museum displays the ropes, ice-axes and expedition relics of Himalayan climbing history, with a viewing telescope trained on Kanchenjunga. For anyone stirred by the mountains outside the window, it is the emotional heart of Darjeeling.

The flat, traffic-free promenade at the town's crown is where Darjeeling has always come to stroll, sit on the benches and watch the light change on the ridge. Ringed by Nathmull's tea shop and Glenary's, it is the town's living room and the natural place to begin and end a day.

A short climb through prayer-flag-draped pines leads to a shrine sacred to both Hindus and Buddhists, where a Shiva lingam and Buddhist bells share the same rock and the views open on all sides. It is the town's oldest sacred spot and quietly moving at any hour.

Darjeeling's oldest church, established in 1843, is a plain grey-stone Scottish kirk with memorial tablets to the planters and soldiers of the Raj still on its walls. A short, evocative stop for anyone drawn to the town's colonial thread.

India's first passenger cable car floats you out over tiers of tea gardens dropping to the Little Rangeet river, the whole Rangeet valley unfolding beneath your feet. A short, scenic glide that gives you the tea country from the air.

A terraced hillside garden crowned by a large Shiva statue, with musical-fountain evenings and one of the town's best framed views of Kanchenjunga across the rooftops. A gentle, well-kept stop a short walk from the heritage hotels.

Opened in 1903, this old collection of Himalayan birds, butterflies and mammals is a curiosity of the Raj-naturalist era, dusty cabinets and all. A quiet, quick detour for the curious, close to the Mall.

The only truly authentic British-Raj heritage property in Darjeeling, a rambling white bungalow of hot-water bottles, coal fires, four-o'clock tea and a music room where time has genuinely stopped. Even for a High Tea or a nightcap it is an experience the town cannot repeat.

Once the summer residence of the Maharaja of Cooch Behar and hotelier since 1887, the Elgin keeps its wood-panelled lounges, manicured lawns and afternoon-tea ritual immaculate. A heritage stay or a leisurely tea here is the polished, comfortable face of old Darjeeling.

Two Raj-era institutions on the same lane: Glenary's for its bakery and the tea room with a valley view, Keventer's for the rooftop breakfast and cold cuts that generations of families have queued for. This is where you taste Darjeeling's colonial-cafe nostalgia over a slow morning.

A working colonial-era garden on a promontory above the Rungeet river where the planter's bungalows have become one of India's most romantic tea retreats, with private guided plucking, factory walks and tastings looking straight at Kanchenjunga. The definitive tea-planter fantasy for a discerning couple or family.

The world's first biodynamic and one of the oldest tea gardens, famous for its moonlight-plucked silver-tips and its immersive tours through the factory and the forest that shades the bushes. A pilgrimage for anyone serious about where great tea comes from.

A steeply terraced Victorian garden of 1878 with orchid houses, a fernery and towering Himalayan conifers, a green pocket of calm just below the bustle of the Mall. An easy, restful walk for a slow afternoon.

A natural rock face used by the mountaineering institute for training and named for Everest's first summiteers, where you can watch aspiring climbers rope up or try a supervised scramble yourself. A short, spirited stop tied to Darjeeling's climbing legend.

The hill town's temperate slopes are one of India's great centres for orchids, gladioli, cacti and gerbera, and the terraced nurseries are a riot of colour and scent you can wander through freely. A gentle, unexpectedly captivating side of the eastern Himalayas.

One of Asia's finest private collections of cacti and succulents, more than fifteen hundred varieties bristling under glass on Atisha Road. A quirky, memorable stop that surprises everyone who thinks they don't care about plants.

The highest point above Kalimpong, a breezy landscaped park where the Teesta winds far below and the whole west-Sikkim snow line stands clear on a good day. A relaxed, panoramic high point that families love for the space and the views.

A 1930s English country mansion, once a jute baron's home and now a heritage bungalow wrapped in pine and rhododendron, thick with Raj-era atmosphere and mist. Worth the visit for its faded colonial romance and the grounds alone.

A sprawling 1900 school campus of stone Scottish-mission buildings and a beautiful chapel spread across the hillside, a serene and storied slice of Kalimpong's missionary heritage. A quiet, atmospheric walk through living history.

A slender lake ringed by pines and orange orchards where you can row a boat, walk the arched footbridge and ride a pony along the water in cool, gentle air. An easy, pretty day trip that suits every generation of a family.

The quieter tea town on the toy-train line, its Eagle's Craig viewpoint looking down over the plains and the Cochrane Place heritage bungalow serving a fine tea. A restful, uncommercialised base deep in the tea country.

Perched at 2,150 m, Pelling gives arguably the closest full-face view of Kanchenjunga anywhere accessible, the whole massif filling your hotel window at first light. The classic base for the west-Sikkim monastery circuit and the mountain romance at its purest.

One of Sikkim's oldest and most important Nyingma monasteries, founded in the 1700s, keeping an extraordinary seven-tiered wooden model of the Buddhist heavens carved by a single monk. A profound, beautifully sited stop with Kanchenjunga as backdrop.

A short forest walk from Pemayangtse leads to the moss-covered ruins of Sikkim's second royal capital, its stone thrones and chortens standing on a ridge above a vast Himalayan drop. Quiet, evocative and beautifully atmospheric.

A sacred wish-fulfilling lake hidden in the forest, so revered that birds are said to lift any leaf that falls on its mirror surface, its shores hung with prayer flags. A serene, spiritual detour on the west-Sikkim loop.

The sleepy first capital of Sikkim, where the coronation throne of the first Chogyal still stands under the pines and the great Kanchenjunga treks begin. A gentle, history-laden village at the foot of the high mountains.

The largest monastery in Sikkim and the seat of the Karmapa's Kagyu lineage, its golden-roofed shrine hall glowing with murals, a jewelled reliquary and rows of chanting monks. The single most important spiritual sight of the Gangtok region.

A high glacial lake at 3,750 m that stays frozen much of the year, ringed by snow with yaks in their festive harness on the shore, an hour and a half's drive from Gangtok on a permit. A dramatic, high-altitude excursion that thrills first-time mountain visitors.

A historic Silk-Road pass on the India-China border at 4,310 m, where you can stand at the frontier fence in the thin cold air with the army post beside you. A stirring, bucket-list drive that needs a special permit and a clear day.

Sikkim's spotless, traffic-free and litter-free central promenade, lined with cafes, tea shops and flower beds and made for an evening stroll. The relaxed social heart of the capital and the natural base for the wider Sikkim circuit.

A vast wilderness of glaciers, alpine lakes and the sacred slopes of Kanchenjunga itself, revered by Sikkimese as a living deity and the setting for the great high treks. Sikkim's crowning wild landscape, entered on permit through Yuksom.

The ridge trek to Sandakphu, West Bengal's highest point at 3,636 m, delivers the fabled 'Sleeping Buddha' line-up of Kanchenjunga with Everest, Lhotse and Makalu ranged beside it. For the adventurous, it is the greatest mountain panorama the region offers, drivable in a rugged Land Rover or walked over days.

A cluster of restored British planter and forest bungalows on a quiet ridge among orange orchards and tea, with sweeping Kanchenjunga views and near-total silence. An intimate, off-the-beaten-track base for travellers who want the hills without the crowds.

A forested, prayer-flag-lined park terraced up to a small sacred pond and monastery, with a Kanchenjunga viewpoint through the pines. A peaceful, uncommercialised stop that breaks the drive between Darjeeling and Kalimpong beautifully.
A single-room Raj-era bar unchanged since 1939 — wood, sofas, old photographs and a whisky by the fire in the oldest heritage hotel in the Himalayas.

venues.a: Dr S. M. Das Road, Darjeeling town
venues.d: Darjeeling's legendary British-style pub — beer, banter and a fire, a fixture of the town's evenings for decades and much-loved by travellers.
The basement bar of the town's grand old café — the go-to for a drink and live music beneath the famous 1880s bakery.
